column1: # HORO-1452: the byte-formatting convention, pinned once for both languages.
# Rust's `reporting::bytes::human_bytes` owns this convention and renders every
# size the CLI reports. The macOS app has to render two figures the CLI never
# sees — the Apply Plan batch estimate and the batch reclaimed total, both sums
# over N single-item invocations with no batch report to carry a rendered
# string — so `GlomerisByteFormat.human` is a port of the same rule.
# A port is only safe while it agrees. Both sides assert against this file:
#   Rust:  src/reporting/bytes.rs, `golden_fixture_pins_the_shared_convention`
#   Swift: macos/GlomerisMenuBar/Tests/GlomerisByteFormatTests.swift
# so a change to either implementation that moves a single rendering fails in
# the language that moved, and a deliberate change to the convention has to be
# made here first and will then fail in the language that has not followed.
# Chosen inputs, and what each one is here to catch:
#   0, 1, 512, 1023        the bare-integer branch, including both its ends
#   1024                   the first scaled value
#   1025                   a value that must round DOWN to a whole unit
#   1280                   an exact .25 tie — proves both sides round half to
#                          even (1.2, not 1.3) rather than one of them rounding
#                          half away from zero
#   1536                   an exact .5 that is not a tie at one decimal place
#   1048575, 1048576       the KB/MB boundary from either side; the first is
#                          deliberately "1024.0 KB", not "1.0 MB", because the
#                          loop tests the unscaled value
#   5242880                the figure from this ticket's own reproduction
#   142300000, 1288490189  the two values Rust's own unit tests already pin
#   1 TB, 1 PB             each remaining unit label is reached at least once
#   u64::MAX               the saturation case — the loop must stop at PB and
#                          not index past the unit table
# Format: <bytes>\t<rendered>. Lines starting with # and blank lines are
# comments. No trailing whitespace: both readers compare the field exactly.
